Graph databases · UC Berkeley DATASCI 205

Who really connects a social network?

We loaded Stanford's SNAP Facebook Social Circles network into Neo4j, added an engagement layer of posts and likes, and used graph algorithms to find the users a campaign should target to maximize reach.

The network

The 3,927 users in the main connected component, positioned by a force-directed layout. Hover a node for details.

Most-connected users

Degree centrality: number of friendships, top 10

These hubs reach the most people directly, so they're natural candidates for seeding a campaign.

Top bridge users

Betweenness centrality: share of shortest paths through each user, top 10

User 1085 sits on 24% of all shortest paths but has only 64 friends. Bridges carry information between communities.

Popular isn't the same as pivotal

Every user: number of friends vs. betweenness centrality

Degree and betweenness are almost uncorrelated (r = 0.10). None of the top-10 hubs is a top-10 bridge, so a reach campaign should target both groups.

How far apart are users?

Average shortest-path length from each ego user to everyone they can reach

Most users are about 4 hops from the central ego users. Lower values mean a more central starting point for spreading content.

Right database for each job

We also scoped how a social platform would split data across database types.

Relationships

Neo4j

Friendships, circles and engagement as a graph, so community detection, influencer search and shortest paths run natively.

Content

MongoDB

User profiles, posts and comments as flexible documents. The schema can change without migrations.

Speed

Redis

In-memory cache for trending posts and popular users, so high-traffic feed lookups stay fast.

UC Berkeley Master of Information and Data Science · DATASCI 205 team project. Data: SNAP Facebook Social Circles (McAuley & Leskovec, Stanford). The posts and likes are a synthetic engagement layer. Centrality computed with NetworkX on the loaded friendship graph. · Source
